pages.transcription:
c/o Viking Press
18 East 48th Street                                Newyork, 27.I.1941.

Dear Hanna & Manfred,
I have had a long talk with Mrs. Salmon today and we
have agreed - in all friendship - that it will be better for both parts if
we find another home for Eva. I find it hard to blame one or the other, it
is just that they are not suited to each other. Mrs. S. told me: "We thought
of taking in a child, but she is just a guest". Mr. S. who apparently tried
very hard in the beginning to gain her confidence, did not succeed, and when
he later tried teasing, apparently this did not turn out too well, either. I
must say that I had not a bad impression of Mrs. S. - quite apart from her not
answering letters and disliking visitors, a point which I did not even mention
when I saw that it was not only our, but also their idea that a separation
might be the best. Eva does not seem to know quite clearly what is wrong,
but I wrote you yesterday, she seemed bored, and she seems to have shown it.
They have not been able to establish a real contact with Eva which they defi-
nitely have tried, and they, too, were somewhat disappointed. If it was any-
one's mistake, it probably was mine, for when Rose Wohl told me that Salmon's
wanted to take a child, she said that they were no intellectuals, and at that
time where our own future was absolutely uncertain and the chances for our re-
turn to USA seemed not too good, I was only concerned in finding a home where
the people really wanted a child and where I felt sure that they would be kind
And that they have been kind to her, and that, if they did not really become
intimate friends, they lived well together and Eva was in no way unhappy,
there can be no doubt, and definitely no harm has been done. I am now trying
to find another home for her and we are thinking that perhaps a boardingschool
might be best for her as in this moment she seems to be in a period where she
does not know what to do with herself and needs stimulation (which I admit she
did not get in S.'s home) as well as some kind of discipline. I am afraid it
is no good that I tell you in detail how and where I try to get information
about a new place. But you may be sure that there is not the slightest need
in transferring her in a hurry and that we will do all our best to ensure that
no further change will be necessary. As to Mr. Haas - (I just now got your
letter of Jan 7th with the address) - I will do all I can to visit the childre
or at least to see him. I have no idea about the distance to Scardale, and at
the present moment the snowstorms make travelling aut to the country somewhat
of an adventure. I am sorry we cannot consult you before making a decision,
but you understand that this is not possible by letter and by cable we could
not give any details. In any case the matter will soon be settled and pro-
bably before you get this letter, Eva will be in new surroundings, this
time chosen deliberatly more with regard to the milieu than it was possible
a few months ago. - By the way, before I finish my report about Eva today,
I only want to say that a short time she sent a letter by boat. I understood
that Mr. Salmon had written you too, and apparently the letter became too
heavy. So do not worry if there should be a gap in the arrival of the
Eva's airmail letters.
We were glad to get your letters to-day and surprised
to hear that Manfred is already about to pass his examination. It is already
the final one? I have no doubt that you will pass it without difficulty, and
I hope that you will both spend a longer period in Bath after that. I have
the idea that I wrote to Raumans some time ago, but I am not quite sure and
will write them again. They are certainly good lodgers and I have no doubt
about Mrs. R.'s cooking. - Have you now settled down completely in Regency
Lodge and where did you put your furniture in Bath? I am glad that Marta can
remain with you and I am sure Smollett's are very content too. - We have
already cabled you that we got the tickets still in time and could use them,
and I hope you did not have too much trouble in arranging all that. We are
glad to have done with flying and sightseeing for a while, and that this time
our rooms look out on a big stone wall, is almost a welcome contrast after
all the beautiful things and views we have seen. We have acclimatised our-
selves very easily to the cold, but find it more difficult to get used to

the central heating. Stefan has not yet begun to work in earnest and I did
not begin working at all. We have rested these days, went to bed extremely
early and only saw very few friends. I went to see Rose Wohl yesterdaybecause
I wanted to get some information. Of course I got quite a different account
of the story about John, but I am inclined to believe it. The trouble was
that John arrived in America with the firm determination to dislike everything
as he had not wanted to come, and they said that for five months nothing had
interested him but the movies and nothing had been good enough for him. And
that they had tried to understand and discuss his way of behaving, seems to
have made the matter worse, for he despised them for it, and from what they
told me behaved as disagreeably as he could, and of course influenced Robin.
Since a fortnight he is with a friend of Carmel's, but they separated quite
peacefully and he comes to see them all the time. Whether he felt happier
there, they did not yet know. I saw Robin coming home from the pictures, and
he looked very well and seemed to feel quite at home. They have slightly
larger flat now, Robin has the one bedroom, Berner's the other and Rose sleeps
in the dining room. I have thought a moment of writing Carmel directly, but I
do not think she would very much appreciate if I just tell her what I had
heard. If you see her, tell her that I met Robin, that he looked well and
quite happy, and that I had gained the impression that Berner's as well as
Rose had done their best. Rose explained her not writing to Carmel by saying
that they were so troubled and did not want to report this while they still
hoped that John might settle down.
We are at the moment considering to go to Newhaven
where the Yale university is, about 1 1/2 hours from New York and good connections
by train. We are both looking forward impatiently to settle down for we are
tired of hotel rooms, restaurant food and above all of the little space
available for working purposes. But I suppose it will be at least another
week before we have settled everything here. I have not the slightest
idea what Newhaven is like, but as long as it is possible to rent a two- or
three room flat furnished for two or three months, I shall be satisfied.

I have told you very much in detail and with all sin-
cerity about Eva and Salmon's to explain the situation, and you may be abso-
lutely certain that there is nothing else behind it. It is nothing wrong
between them, there have been no incidents and no quarrels, it is only the
difference of milieu - he likes football and fun- which makes them not abso-
lutely suited to each other. There is nothing we have hidden from you and
nothing for you to worry about. And now we are near and we still have not
given up our guardianship and do not intend to do so. All we want you to
do is to keep well and fresh and to look after our house in Bath by spending
as much of your time there as you possibly can.

Fondest love and kisses,
kindest regards to all the friends,

Lotte.
